newsitem.title: USA: Time running out for Ahmanson in bid for Great Western.
newsitem.headline: Time running out for Ahmanson in bid for Great Western.

text.p: Great Western Financial Corp. Tuesday rejected a hostile bid by H.F. Ahmanson and Co., which may be forced to raise its offer in order to stay in the race to buy the rival California savings and loan.
"Time is running out for Ahmanson. Its premium is not enough to carry the day. The only thing left for Ahmanson to do is to raise its bid," said Thomas O'Donnell, analyst with Smith Barney.
In recent sessions, the value of Irwindale, Calif.-based Ahmanson's bid to swap 1.2 of its shares for Great Western has slipped below a friendly offer by Seattle-based Washington Mutual Inc.
In an effort to thwart Ahmanson's hostile bid, Great Western, based in Chatsworth, Calif., agreed to merge with Washington Mutual in early March.
Under that deal, Washington Mutual would swap 0.9 of its shares for each Great Western share.
Both bids are worth about $7 billion, with Ahmanson's bid valued at $50.40 a share and Washington Mutual's at $50.52 a share in late trading Tuesday.
Ahmanson, the parent of Home Savings of America, one of the nation's largest consumer banks, declined comment Tuesday on whether it would change its offer.
In an interview last week, Ahmanson Chief Executive Officer Charles Rinehart said, "There's no reason to change our offer. We think we'll get the response (to our offer)."
"They're both competitive bids, but what has swung this in Washington Mutual's direction is the endorsement of the Great Western board," Smith Barney's O'Donnell said.

"There's a pretty strong indication that shareholders are favoring Washington Mutual," said David Winton, analyst with Keefe Bruyette Woods, who said Washington Mutual's broader franchise gives it an edge.
"It has a franchise from Seattle to California, rather than one just exclusively in California," said Winton, referring to Ahmanson.

On Tuesday, Great Western's board reaffirmed its commitment to merge with Washington Mutual and urged stockholders not to tender their shares to Ahmanson, which is planning to take its offer directly to the shareholders in an exchange offer, pending Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approval.
Ahmanson responded by saying its plan to proceed with the exchange offer was a response to the refusal by Great Western's board to negotiate.
But analysts note that raising its offer could backfire for Ahmanson.

"They could raise their bid but (Wall) Street just might start to balk and they'd be pushing the envelope. It gets to a point where they'd be perceived as paying too much for Great Western," said Winton.

Ahmanson has been trying to delay a shareholder vote on Washington Mutual's proposal to give the Great Western board a chance to hear from any new boardmembers that are elected at Great Western's annual meeting on June 13.
Ahmanson is seeking to have three directors elected to the board.

"In sharp contrast to Ahmanson's unsolicited proposal, our merger with Washington Mutual makes compelling economic and strategic sense for Great Western stockholders," Great Western said in a statement.
"We remain strongly committed to our merger with Washington Mutual and look forward to the June 13 stockholder vote."
Great Western's stock rose 50 cents to $47.625, while Ahmanson gained 62.5 cents to $42.125 on the New York Stock Exchange. Washington Mutual rose 12.5 cents to $56 on Nasdaq.
